question: Under the TSI INF, what are the immediate action limits for track gauge as an isolated defect on 1 435 mm track for a line speed of 140 km/h?
answer:
Under the TSI INF, for a line speed of 140 km/h (speed range $120 < v \le 160$ km/h), the immediate action limits for track gauge as an isolated defect on standard track gauge are set out in Table 12 [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.4]:

* **Minimum track gauge:** 1 427 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.4]
* **Maximum track gauge:** 1 470 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.4]

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Commission Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014, TSI for the 'infrastructure' subsystem (TSI INF) | Annex > 4. DESCRIPTION OF THE INFRASTRUCTURE SUBSYSTEM > 4.2. Functional and technical specifications of subsystem > 4.2.8. Immediate action limits on track geometry defects > 4.2.8.3. The immediate action limit for track twist
(1) The immediate action limit for track twist as an isolated defect is given as a zero to peak value. Track twist is defined in EN 13848-1:2003+A1:2008 point 4.6.
(2) The track twist limit is a function of the measurement base applied according to EN 13848-5:2008+A1:2010 point 8.6.
(3) The infrastructure manager shall set out in the maintenance plan the base-length on which it will measure the track in order to check compliance with this requirement. The base-length of measurement shall include at least one base between 2 and 5 m.
(4) Instead of points (1) and (2), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the track twist, for a base length of 10 m, shall be not more than:
(a) 16 mm for passenger lines with v > 120 km/h or freight lines with v > 80 km/h
(b) 20 mm for passenger lines with v ≤ 120 km/h or freight lines with v ≤ 80 km/h
(5) Instead of point (3), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the Infrastructure Manager shall set out in the maintenance plan the base-length on which it will measure the track in order to check compliance with this requirement. The base-length of measurement shall include at least one base of 10 m.
(6) Instead of point (2), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, the track twist limit is a function of the measurement base applied according to one of the following equations depending on the cant:
(a) Twist limit = (20/l + 3) for u ≤ 0,67 × (r – 100) with a maximum value of:
7 mm/m for speeds v ≤ 200 km/h, 5 mm/m for speed v > 200 km/h
(b) Twist limit = (20/l + 1,5) for 0,67 × (r – 100) < u < 0,9 × (r – 50) with a maximum value of:
6 mm/m for l ≤ 5 m, 3 mm/m for l > 13 m
u = cant (mm), l = twist base length (m), r = horizontal curve radius (m)

question: What is the maximum cant allowed in service on standard 1 435 mm lines, on dedicated passenger lines, and on the 1 668 mm track gauge system?
answer:
According to the TSI Infrastructure (TSI INF), the immediate action limits for the maximum cant allowed in service are:

* **Standard lines (general rule):** 180 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.5].
* **Dedicated passenger traffic lines:** 190 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.5].
* **1 668 mm track gauge system:** 200 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.5].

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

Commission Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014, TSI for the 'infrastructure' subsystem (TSI INF) | Annex > 4. DESCRIPTION OF THE INFRASTRUCTURE SUBSYSTEM > 4.2. Functional and technical specifications of subsystem > 4.2.4. Track parameters > 4.2.4.2. Cant
(1) The design cant for lines shall be limited as defined in Table 7.
Table 7 - Design cant [mm]
| Freight and mixed traffic | Passenger traffic
Ballasted track | 160 | 180
Non ballasted track | 170 | 180
(2) The design cant on tracks adjacent to station platforms where trains are intended to stop in normal service shall not exceed 110 mm.
(3) New lines with mixed or freight traffic on curves with a radius less than 305 m and a cant transition steeper than 1 mm/m, the cant shall be restricted to the limit given by the following formula
D ≤ (R – 50)/1,5
where D is the cant in mm and R is the radius in m.
(4) Instead of points (1) to (3), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the design cant shall not exceed 150 mm.
(5) Instead of point (1), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, the design cant shall not exceed 180 mm.
(6) Instead of point (2), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, the design cant on tracks adjacent to station platforms where trains are intended to stop in normal service shall not exceed 125 mm.
(7) Instead of point (3), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, for new lines with mixed or freight traffic on curves with a radius less than 250 m, the cant shall be restricted to the limit given by the following formula:
D ≤ 0,9 * (R – 50)
where D is the cant in mm and R is the radius in m.
(8) Instead of point (1), for the 1 600 mm track gauge system the design cant shall not exceed 185 mm.

question: What are the in-service minimum flangeway width and minimum flangeway depth for switches and crossings on 1 435 mm track?
answer:
For switches and crossings on standard track gauge systems (1 435 mm track), the in-service immediate action limits are:

* **Minimum flangeway width:** 38 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.6(1)-(2)]
* **Minimum flangeway depth:** 40 mm [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.6(1)-(2)]

(1) The technical characteristics of switches and crossings shall comply with the following in-service values:
(a) Maximum value of free wheel passage in switches: 1 380 mm.
This value can be increased if the infrastructure manager demonstrates that the actuation and locking system of the switch is able to resist the lateral impact forces of a wheelset.

This value is measured 14 mm below the running surface, and on the theoretical reference line, at an appropriate distance back from the actual point (RP) of the nose as indicated in Figure 2.

(e) Minimum flangeway width: 38 mm.
(f) Minimum flangeway depth: 40 mm.
(g) Maximum height of check rail: 70 mm.
(2) All relevant requirements for switches and crossings are also applicable to other technical solutions using switch rails, for example side modifiers used in multi-rail track.

question: What is the maximum in-service free wheel passage in switches on 1 435 mm track, and under what condition may it be exceeded?
answer:
For switches on standard track gauge (1 435 mm), the maximum in-service value of free wheel passage in switches is **1 380 mm** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.6(1)-(2)].

This value may be increased if the infrastructure manager demonstrates that the actuation and locking system of the switch is able to resist the lateral impact forces of a wheelset [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.6(1)-(2)].

question: What must an infrastructure manager's maintenance file contain at a minimum under the TSI INF?
answer:
Under point 4.5.1 of the TSI INF Annex, an infrastructure manager's maintenance file must contain at least the following items related to track geometric quality and limits on isolated defects:

1. **A set of values for immediate action limits** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5.1].
2. **The measures taken** (for example, speed restriction, repair time) **when prescribed limits are not met** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5.1].

In addition, the maintenance file must be prepared before placing a line into service as part of the technical file accompanying the declaration of verification [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5]. 

*(Note: Point 4.5.2 specifies additional minimum requirements for the infrastructure manager's overall maintenance plan, which includes the contents of the maintenance file along with intervention and alert limits, staff competences and safety methods, protection rules, and checking means [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5.2].)*

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: What is the difference between an alert limit, an intervention limit and an immediate action limit for track geometry?
answer:
According to Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014 (TSI INF), the three track geometry limits are defined by the level of maintenance or operational response required when exceeded:

* **Alert limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires that the track geometry condition is analysed and considered in the regularly planned maintenance operations [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 1/5)].
* **Intervention limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires corrective maintenance in order that the immediate action limit shall not be reached before the next inspection [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 3/5)].
* **Immediate action limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires taking measures to reduce the risk of derailment to an acceptable level [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 3/5)].

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Commission Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014, TSI for the 'infrastructure' subsystem (TSI INF) | Annex > 4. DESCRIPTION OF THE INFRASTRUCTURE SUBSYSTEM > 4.2. Functional and technical specifications of subsystem > 4.2.8. Immediate action limits on track geometry defects > 4.2.8.3. The immediate action limit for track twist
(1) The immediate action limit for track twist as an isolated defect is given as a zero to peak value. Track twist is defined in EN 13848-1:2003+A1:2008 point 4.6.
(2) The track twist limit is a function of the measurement base applied according to EN 13848-5:2008+A1:2010 point 8.6.
(3) The infrastructure manager shall set out in the maintenance plan the base-length on which it will measure the track in order to check compliance with this requirement. The base-length of measurement shall include at least one base between 2 and 5 m.
(4) Instead of points (1) and (2), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the track twist, for a base length of 10 m, shall be not more than:
(a) 16 mm for passenger lines with v > 120 km/h or freight lines with v > 80 km/h
(b) 20 mm for passenger lines with v ≤ 120 km/h or freight lines with v ≤ 80 km/h
(5) Instead of point (3), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the Infrastructure Manager shall set out in the maintenance plan the base-length on which it will measure the track in order to check compliance with this requirement. The base-length of measurement shall include at least one base of 10 m.
(6) Instead of point (2), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, the track twist limit is a function of the measurement base applied according to one of the following equations depending on the cant:
(a) Twist limit = (20/l + 3) for u ≤ 0,67 × (r – 100) with a maximum value of:
7 mm/m for speeds v ≤ 200 km/h, 5 mm/m for speed v > 200 km/h
(b) Twist limit = (20/l + 1,5) for 0,67 × (r – 100) < u < 0,9 × (r – 50) with a maximum value of:
6 mm/m for l ≤ 5 m, 3 mm/m for l > 13 m
u = cant (mm), l = twist base length (m), r = horizontal curve radius (m)

The infrastructure manager shall have a maintenance plan containing the items listed in point 4.5.1 together with at least the following items related to the same elements:

(b) a statement about the methods, professional competences of staff and personal protective safety equipment necessary to be used,

According to Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014 (TSI INF), the three track geometry limits are defined by the level of maintenance or operational response required when exceeded:

* **Alert limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires that the track geometry condition is analysed and considered in the regularly planned maintenance operations [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 1/5)].
* **Intervention limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires corrective maintenance in order that the immediate action limit shall not be reached before the next inspection [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 3/5)].
* **Immediate action limit:** The value which, if exceeded, requires taking measures to reduce the risk of derailment to an acceptable level [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix S (part 3/5)].

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: What measurement base length must the infrastructure manager include when checking track twist against the immediate action limit, for 1 435 mm and for 1 520 mm track?
answer:
When checking track twist against the immediate action limit, the infrastructure manager must set out the measurement base length in the maintenance plan according to the following requirements:

* **For standard track (1 435 mm gauge):** The measurement base-length must include at least one base **between 2 and 5 m** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.3].
* **For the 1 520 mm track gauge system:** The measurement base-length must include at least one base of **10 m** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.3]. *(Note: Specific network cases exist, such as in Poland and Slovakia, where the 2 to 5 m base requirements apply instead for 1 520 mm gauge [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.7.12.7], [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.7.19.5]).*

question: What mechanical requirements must rail steel meet to qualify as the 'rail' interoperability constituent?
answer:
To qualify as the ‘rail’ interoperability constituent, the rail steel must meet the following mechanical requirements [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.1.2]:

* **Rail hardness:** at least 200 HBW [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.1.2].
* **Tensile strength:** at least 680 MPa [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.1.2].
* **Fatigue resistance:** minimum of 5 × 10⁶ cycles at fatigue test without failure [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.1.2].

Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: What longitudinal slip resistance and fatigue performance must a rail fastening system achieve in laboratory tests?
answer:
Under laboratory test conditions, a rail fastening system must meet the following requirements:

* **Longitudinal slip resistance:** The longitudinal force required to cause the rail to begin to slip (i.e. move in an inelastic way) through a single rail fastening assembly must be at least 7 kN, and at least 9 kN for line speeds exceeding 250 km/h [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.2].
* **Fatigue performance:** The rail fastening system must resist the application of 3,000,000 cycles of the typical load applied in a sharp curve [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.2]. Following this test:
  * Its performance in terms of clamping force and longitudinal restraint must not degrade by more than 20% [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.2].
  * Its vertical stiffness must not degrade by more than 25% [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.2].
  * The typical test load must be appropriate to the maximum axle load the fastening system is designed to accommodate, as well as the specific combination of rail, rail inclination, rail pad, and sleeper type used with it [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.3.2].

Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: Which track components are interoperability constituents under the TSI INF, and do rails and sleepers in switches and crossings count?
answer:
Under Section 5.2 of the TSI INF Annex, only the following elements are declared to be interoperability constituents [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.2]:
* The rail [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.2]
* The rail fastening systems [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.2]
* Track sleepers [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.2]

**Switches and crossings:** No, rails, fastenings, and sleepers used for short lengths of track for specific purposes—such as in switches and crossings, expansion devices, transition slabs, and special structures—are **not** considered to be interoperability constituents [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 5.2].

question: When can a track design be treated as an 'existing track design' to give presumption of conformity for track resistance?
answer:
To demonstrate conformity for track resistance (plain line) by reference to an existing track design, the design must meet the operating conditions intended for the subsystem concerned [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.2.5.1(1)]. 

A track design is considered to be **existing** if both of the following conditions are met:
1. The track design has been in normal operation for at least one year [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.2.5.1(3)(a)]; and
2. The total tonnage over the track was at least 20 million gross tons for the period of normal operation [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.2.5.1(3)(b)].

To confirm an existing track design, it must be checked that its technical characteristics (Appendix C.1 to the TSI) and operating conditions applied in normal operation (Appendix D.1 to the TSI) are specified, and that reference to the previous use of the track design is available [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.2.5.1(2), (4), (5)].

question: If we replace worn rails like-for-like during routine maintenance, do we need an EC verification and an authorisation for placing in service?
answer:
**No**, you do not need an EC verification or an authorisation for placing in service when replacing worn rails like-for-like during routine maintenance.

* **No authorisation or EC verification for maintenance:** Where parts of an infrastructure subsystem are maintained, formal verification and authorisation for placing into service are not required `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.3]`. Directive (EU) 2016/797 categorises replacing components with parts of identical function and performance in the framework of preventive or corrective maintenance as "substitution in the framework of maintenance" `[Dir_2016_797, Article 2(13)-(22)]`. Authorisation for placing in service and EC verification procedures apply to new subsystems or to the renewal and upgrading of existing subsystems, not routine maintenance `[Dir_2016_797, Article 15(1)-(5)]`, `[Dir_2016_797, Article 18(1)-(4)]`, `[Dir_2016_797, Article 18(5)-(6)]`.
* **Maintenance responsibilities:** Even though formal verification and authorisation are not required, maintenance replacements should, as far as reasonably practicable, be undertaken in accordance with the TSI INF requirements `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.3]`. The body responsible for maintenance must ensure that replacement components are suitable for their applications, used within their area of use, traceable, and meet essential requirements `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.5.3]`, `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.6.3]`.

Directive (EU) 2016/797 on the interoperability of the rail system within the European Union (recast) | Chapter IV: Subsystems > Article 15: Procedure for establishing the ‘EC’ declaration of verification
1. In order to establish the ‘EC’ declaration of verification necessary for placing on the market and placing in service referred to in Chapter V, the applicant shall request the conformity assessment body or bodies that it has selected for that purpose to apply the ‘EC’ verification procedure set out in Annex IV.
2. The applicant shall establish the ‘EC’ declaration of verification of a subsystem. The applicant shall declare on his sole responsibility that the subsystem concerned has been subject to the relevant verification procedures and that it satisfies the requirements of relevant Union law and any relevant national rule. The ‘EC’ declaration of verification and the accompanying documents shall be dated and signed by the applicant.
3. The task of the notified body responsible for the ‘EC’ verification of a subsystem shall begin at the design stage and cover the entire manufacturing period through to the acceptance stage before the subsystem is placed on the market or in service. It shall, in accordance with the relevant TSI, also cover verification of the interfaces of the subsystem in question with the system into which it is incorporated.
4. The applicant shall be responsible for compiling the technical file that is to accompany the ‘EC’ declaration of verification. That technical file shall contain all the necessary documents relating to the characteristics of the subsystem and, where appropriate, all the documents certifying conformity of the interoperability constituents. It shall also contain all the elements relating to the conditions and limits of use and to the instructions concerning servicing, constant or routine monitoring, adjustment and maintenance.
5. In the event of the renewal or upgrading of a subsystem resulting in an amendment to the technical file and affecting the validity of the verification procedures already carried out, the applicant shall assess the need for a new ‘EC’ declaration of verification.

draft_answer:
**No**, you do not need an EC verification or an authorisation for placing in service when replacing worn rails like-for-like during routine maintenance.

* **No authorisation or EC verification for maintenance:** Where parts of an infrastructure subsystem are maintained, formal verification and authorisation for placing into service are not required `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.3]`. Directive (EU) 2016/797 categorises replacing components with parts of identical function and performance in the framework of preventive or corrective maintenance as "substitution in the framework of maintenance" `[Dir_2016_797, Article 2(13)-(22)]`. Authorisation for placing in service and EC verification procedures apply to new subsystems or to the renewal and upgrading of existing subsystems, not routine maintenance `[Dir_2016_797, Article 15(1)-(5)]`, `[Dir_2016_797, Article 18(1)-(4)]`, `[Dir_2016_797, Article 18(5)-(6)]`.
* **Maintenance responsibilities:** Even though formal verification and authorisation are not required, maintenance replacements should, as far as reasonably practicable, be undertaken in accordance with the TSI INF requirements `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.3]`. The body responsible for maintenance must ensure that replacement components are suitable for their applications, used within their area of use, traceable, and meet essential requirements `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.5.3]`, `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 6.6.3]`.

question: When is the infrastructure subsystem of a line considered 'upgraded' rather than renewed under the TSI INF?
answer:
Under the TSI INF, the infrastructure subsystem of a line is distinguished between upgrading and renewal as follows:

* **Upgrading** means any major modification work on a subsystem or part of a subsystem which improves the overall performance of the subsystem [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.1]. In the specific context of the TSI INF, the infrastructure subsystem of a line is considered to be upgraded when at least the performance parameters **axle load** or **gauge** are changed in order to meet the requirements of another traffic code [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.1].
* **Renewal** means any major substitution work on a subsystem or part of a subsystem which does not change the overall performance of the subsystem [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.2]. Renewal is the same case as upgrading, but without a change in performance parameters [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 7.3.2].

(1) In accordance with Article 2(n) of Directive 2008/57/EC, ‘renewal’ means any major substitution work on a subsystem or part subsystem which does not change the overall performance of the subsystem.
(2) For this purpose major substitution should be interpreted as a project undertaken to systematically replace elements of a line or a section of a line. Renewal differs from a substitution in the framework of maintenance, referred to in point 7.3.3 below, since it gives the opportunity to achieve a TSI compliant route. A renewal is the same case as upgrading, but without a change in performance parameters.
(3) Where article 20(2) of Directive 2008/57/EC applies because the renewal is subject of an authorisation of placing into service, Member States shall decide which requirements of the TSI must be applied.
(4) Where article 20(2) of Directive 2008/57/EC does not apply because the renewal is not subject of an authorisation of placing into service, the conformity with this TSI is recommended. Where compliance is not possible to reach, the contracting entity informs the Member State of the reasons thereof.
(5) For a project including elements not being TSI compliant, the procedures for the assessment of conformity and EC verification to be applied should be agreed with the Member State.

Commission Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014, TSI for the 'infrastructure' subsystem (TSI INF) | Annex > 2. DEFINITION AND SCOPE OF SUBSYSTEM > 2.1. Definition of the infrastructure subsystem
This TSI covers:
(a) the infrastructure structural subsystem
(b) the part of the maintenance functional subsystem relating to the infrastructure subsystem (that is: washing plants for external cleaning of trains, water restocking, refuelling, fixed installations for toilet discharge and electrical shore supplies).
The elements of the infrastructure subsystem are described in Annex II (2.1. Infrastructure) to Directive 2008/57/EC.
The scope of this TSI therefore includes the following aspects of the infrastructure subsystem:
(a) Line layout,
(b) Track parameters,
(c) Switches and crossings,
(d) Track resistance to applied loads,
(e) Structures resistance to traffic loads,
(f) Immediate action limits on track geometry defects,
(g) Platforms,
(h) Health, safety and environment,
(i) Provision for operation,
(j) Fixed installations for servicing trains.
Further details are set out in point 4.2.2 of this TSI.

retrieved_chunks.text:
Commission Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014, TSI for the 'infrastructure' subsystem (TSI INF) | Article 2: Scope
1. The TSI shall apply to all new, upgraded or renewed ‘infrastructure’ of the rail system in the European Union as defined in point 2.1 of Annex I to Directive 2008/57/EC.
2. Without prejudice to Articles 7 and 8 and point 7.2 of the Annex, the TSI shall apply to new railway lines in the European Union, which are placed in service from 1 January 2015.
3. The TSI shall not apply to existing infrastructure of the rail system in the European Union, which is already placed in service on all or part of the network of any Member State on 1 January 2015, except when it is subject to renewal or upgrading in accordance with Article 20 of Directive 2008/57/EC and Section 7.3 of the Annex.
4. The TSI shall apply to the following networks:
(a) the trans-European conventional rail system network as defined in Annex I, point 1.1 to Directive 2008/57/EC;
(b) the trans-European high-speed rail system network (TEN) as defined in Annex I, point 2.1 to Directive 2008/57/EC;
(c) other parts of the network of the rail system in the Union;
and excludes the cases referred to in Article 1(3) of Directive 2008/57/EC.
5. The TSI shall apply to networks with the following nominal track gauges: 1 435 mm, 1 520 mm, 1 524 mm, 1 600 mm and 1 668 mm.
6. Metric gauge is excluded from the technical scope of this TSI.
7. The technical and geographical scope of this Regulation is set out in Sections 1.1 and 1.2 of the Annex.

question: What is the maximum design cant on ballasted track for mixed traffic versus passenger traffic, and next to platforms where trains stop?
answer:
According to the TSI for the infrastructure subsystem (TSI INF):

* **Ballasted track design cant limits:**
  * **Freight and mixed traffic:** Maximum **160 mm** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.4.2].
  * **Passenger traffic:** Maximum **180 mm** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.4.2].

* **Tracks adjacent to station platforms (normal stopping service):**
  * Maximum **110 mm** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.4.2] (or **125 mm** for the 1 668 mm track gauge system [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.4.2]).

question: Ride instability has been reported on a section where trains run at 200 km/h. What does the infrastructure manager measure and what equivalent conicity limit applies?
answer:
When ride instability is reported, the infrastructure manager must undertake the following steps [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.11.2(1)]:

* **What to measure:** The infrastructure manager shall measure the **track gauge** and the **railhead profiles** at the site in question at intervals of approximately 10 m [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.11.2(2)].
* **Calculation:** The mean equivalent conicity over 100 m is calculated by modelling with the specified reference wheelsets [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.11.2(2)].
* **Limit value:** For a section operating at 200 km/h (which falls in the speed range 160 < v ≤ 230 km/h), the maximum limit value for the mean equivalent conicity over 100 m is **0.30** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.11.2(2)].

> Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: What minimum ballast depth under the sleeper does the TSI INF require?
answer:
The TSI INF (Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014) does not specify a fixed numerical minimum ballast depth under the sleeper. 

Instead, the regulation sets the following requirements for track design:
* Appendix C.1 mandates that track design must be defined by technical characteristics that include the ballast cross sections (specifically ballast shoulder and ballast thickness) [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, Appendix C.1].
* The overall track design must be engineered to withstand vertical loads [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.6.1], longitudinal forces [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.6.2.1], and lateral forces [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.6.3].

Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: What is the immediate action limit for isolated alignment defects on a line running at 320 km/h?
answer:
Under Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014 (TSI INF), the immediate action limits for isolated defects in alignment for speeds of more than 300 km/h (which includes 320 km/h) are an **open point** [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.1]. 

For speeds up to 300 km/h, the limits are set out in point 8.5 of EN 13848-5:2008+A1:2010 (within wavelength range D1 as set out in Table 6 of that standard) [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.1].

question: Which track-related precursors to accidents must be reported as common safety indicators, and how is a 'broken rail' defined?
answer:
The track-related precursors to accidents that must be reported as common safety indicators (CSIs) are:
* **Broken rail** [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, 4]
* **Track buckle and other track misalignment** [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, 4]

All precursors must be reported, regardless of whether or not they result in accidents [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, 4].

### Definition of 'broken rail'
A **broken rail** is defined as any rail which is separated into two or more pieces, or any rail from which a piece of metal becomes detached, causing a gap of more than 50 mm in length and more than 10 mm in depth on the running surface [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 4].

question: What thresholds turn a railway accident into a 'serious accident' under the Railway Safety Directive?
answer:
Under Directive (EU) 2016/798, a **"serious accident"** means any train collision or derailment of trains resulting in at least one of the following thresholds, or any other accident with the same consequences which has an obvious impact on railway safety regulation or safety management [Dir_2016_798, Article 3(9)-(17)]:

* **Fatalities**: The death of at least one person [Dir_2016_798, Article 3(9)-(17)] (defined as dying immediately or within 30 days as a result of the accident, excluding suicide [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 1.10-1.19]).
* **Serious injuries**: Serious injuries to 5 or more persons [Dir_2016_798, Article 3(9)-(17)] (defined as hospitalization for more than 24 hours, excluding attempted suicide [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 1.10-1.19]).
* **Extensive damage**: Extensive damage to rolling stock, infrastructure, or the environment [Dir_2016_798, Article 3(9)-(17)], where "extensive damage" is specifically defined as damage that can be immediately assessed by the investigating body to cost **at least EUR 2 million in total** [Dir_2016_798, Article 3(9)-(17)].

(38) A safety investigation should be kept separate from any judicial inquiry into the same incident, and those conducting it should be granted access to evidence and witnesses. The body should function in a way which avoids any conflict of interest and any possible involvement in the causes of the occurrences that are investigated. In particular, its functional independence should not be affected if it is closely linked, for organisational and legal structure purposes, to the national safety authority, the Agency or the regulator of railways. Its investigations should be carried out with as much openness as possible. For each occurrence, the investigating body should establish the relevant investigation group possessing the expertise needed to find the immediate and underlying causes.
(39) An investigation after a serious accident should be carried out in such a way that all parties are given the possibility to be heard and to share the results. In particular, during the investigation, the investigating body should update the parties whom it judges as having safety-related responsibility on the progress of the investigation, and should take account of their views and opinions. This will allow the investigating body to receive any additional relevant information and to be aware of different opinions on its work so that it can complete its investigation in the most appropriate manner. Such consultation should in no case lead to apportioning blame or liability but, rather, to collecting factual evidence and learning lessons for the future improvement of safety. The investigating body should, however, be free to choose the information it intends to share with such parties in order to avoid any undue pressure, except when this is requested by those conducting the judicial procedure. The investigating body should also take account of the reasonable information needs of any victims and of their relatives.

question: What makes an accident 'significant' for the common safety indicators, and what counts as significant damage and extensive traffic disruption?
answer:
For the common safety indicators (CSIs), the relevant terms are defined as follows:

* **Significant accident:** Any accident involving at least one rail vehicle in motion, resulting in at least one killed or seriously injured person, or in significant damage to stock, track, other installations or environment, or extensive disruptions to traffic, excluding accidents in workshops, warehouses, and depots [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 1.1-1.9].
* **Significant damage to stock, track, other installations or environment:** Damage that is equivalent to EUR 150 000 or more [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 1.1-1.9].
* **Extensive disruptions to traffic:** Suspension of train services on a main railway line for six hours or more [Dir_2016_798, Annex I, Appendix, 1.1-1.9].

question: After a serious accident, what are the investigating body's deadlines for deciding on the investigation, informing the Agency, and publishing the final report?
answer:
According to Directive (EU) 2016/798, the deadlines for the investigating body are as follows:

* **Decision on opening an investigation:** The investigating body must decide whether or not to start an investigation without delay and no later than **2 months** after receiving the notification of the accident or incident [Dir_2016_798, Article 22(1)-(4)].
* **Informing the Agency (ERA):** The investigating body must inform the Agency within **7 days** of deciding to open an investigation [Dir_2016_798, Article 25]. It must also send a copy of the final report to the Agency [Dir_2016_798, Article 25].
* **Publishing the final report:** The final report must be made public in the shortest possible time and normally no later than **12 months** after the date of the occurrence [Dir_2016_798, Article 24]. If it cannot be published within 12 months, the investigating body must release an interim statement at least on each anniversary of the accident [Dir_2016_798, Article 24].

question: How long is an infrastructure manager's safety authorisation valid, and when must it be revised?
answer:
An infrastructure manager's safety authorisation is subject to the following rules regarding validity and revision:

* **Validity:** A safety authorisation is valid for **5 years** and may be renewed upon application by the infrastructure manager [Dir_2016_798, Article 12(2)].
* **Mandatory revision:** It must be wholly or partly revised whenever **substantial changes** are made to the infrastructure, signalling, or energy subsystems, or to the principles of their operation and maintenance [Dir_2016_798, Article 12(2)]. The infrastructure manager must inform the national safety authority of all such changes without delay [Dir_2016_798, Article 12(2)].
* **Revision requested by the authority:** The national safety authority may require the safety authorisation to be revised following **substantial changes to the safety regulatory framework** [Dir_2016_798, Article 12(2)].

Note: based on the acts as originally published (later amendments not included). Not legal advice; for binding decisions check the consolidated text on EUR-Lex.

question: For the renewal or upgrading of an existing fixed subsystem, what does the applicant send to the national safety authority, and on what criteria and timeline does it decide whether a new authorisation is needed?
answer:
In the event of the renewal or upgrading of an existing fixed subsystem, the rules regarding submission, timeline, and decision criteria are as follows:

* **What the applicant sends:** The applicant must send a file describing the project to the national safety authority [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)].
* **Timeline:**
  * Within **one month** of receipt of the request, the national safety authority must inform the applicant whether the file is complete or ask for relevant supplementary information, setting a reasonable deadline for providing it [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)].
  * The national safety authority must decide whether a new authorisation for placing in service is needed within a predetermined, reasonable time, and in any case **within four months** of receipt of all relevant information [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)].
* **Criteria for decision:** The national safety authority (in close cooperation with the Agency for trackside ERTMS projects) decides whether a new authorisation is required based on whether:
  1. The overall safety level of the subsystem concerned may be adversely affected by the envisaged works [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)];
  2. It is required by the relevant TSIs [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)];
  3. It is required by the national implementation plans established by the Member States [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)]; or
  4. Changes are made to the values of the parameters on the basis of which the authorisation was originally granted [Dir_2016_797, Article 18(6)].

question: After a natural disaster damages a line, can a Member State allow restoration works without applying the TSIs, and for how long?
answer:
Yes. Following an accident or a natural disaster, a Member State may allow an applicant not to apply one or more TSIs (or parts of them) if the conditions for the rapid restoration of the network do not economically or technically allow for partial or total application of the relevant TSIs [Dir_2016_797, Article 7(1)-(3)].

Regarding the duration and procedure:
* The non-application of the TSIs must be limited to the period before the restoration of the network [Dir_2016_797, Article 7(1)-(3)].
* The Member State concerned must communicate to the European Commission its decision not to apply one or more TSIs or parts of them [Dir_2016_797, Article 7(1)-(3)].

question: What are the four maintenance functions of an entity in charge of maintenance, which may be outsourced, and how long is an ECM certificate valid?
answer:
The four maintenance functions of an entity in charge of maintenance (ECM) are:

1. **Management function:** to supervise and coordinate the maintenance functions and ensure the safe state of the vehicle in the railway system [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)]. The ECM must carry out this function itself; it cannot be outsourced [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)].
2. **Maintenance development function:** responsible for managing the maintenance documentation (including configuration management) based on design, operational data, performance, and return on experience [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)]. This function (or parts of it) may be outsourced [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)] [Reg_2019_779, Article 9(1)].
3. **Fleet-maintenance management function:** to manage the vehicle's removal for maintenance and its return to operation after maintenance [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)]. This function (or parts of it) may be outsourced [Dir_2016_798, Article 14(3)] [Reg_2019_779, Article 9(1)].

question: When is ECM certification mandatory under Implementing Regulation 2019/779, and does an infrastructure manager maintaining its own on-track machines need one?
answer:
Under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/779, ECM certification is mandatory for any entity in charge of maintenance (ECM) that:

* Is responsible for the maintenance of freight wagons [Reg_2019_779, Article 3]; or
* Is **not** a railway undertaking or an infrastructure manager maintaining vehicles exclusively for its own operations [Reg_2019_779, Article 3].

### Maintenance of on-track machines by an infrastructure manager

* **No**, an ECM certification is not mandatory for an infrastructure manager maintaining vehicles (such as on-track machines or infrastructure inspection vehicles) exclusively for its own operations, unless they are freight wagons [Reg_2019_779, Article 3].
* Instead, the infrastructure manager can demonstrate compliance with the Annex II maintenance requirements through its **safety authorisation** process [Reg_2019_779, Article 3], as assessing its capacity to operate vehicles for infrastructure maintenance forms part of the safety authorisation assessment under Directive (EU) 2016/798 [Reg_2019_779, Recitals 10-13].
* However, the infrastructure manager may still voluntarily choose to apply for an ECM certification [Reg_2019_779, Article 3].

question: What fine does Spain impose on an infrastructure manager that fails to submit its annual safety report on time?
answer:
The corpus does not cover this question.

Directive (EU) 2016/798 requires infrastructure managers to submit an annual safety report to their national safety authority before 31 May of each year [Dir_2016_798, Article 9(6)-(7)] and mandates that Member States lay down rules on effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties for infringements [Dir_2016_798, Article 30]. However, the specific fine amounts established under Spanish national law are not contained in the corpus.

To determine the specific fine imposed in Spain, check Spanish national railway law (such as the *Ley 38/2015 del Sector Ferroviario*) or consult Spain's national safety authority (*Agencia Estatal de Seguridad Ferroviaria* — AESF).

question: What immediate action limit for isolated longitudinal level defects (wavelength range D1) applies on a line running at 200 km/h?
answer:
Under Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014 (TSI INF), immediate action limits for isolated defects in longitudinal level (wavelength range D1) are set out in point 8.3 and Table 5 of European Standard EN 13848-5:2008+A1:2010 `[Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.2.8.2]`.

The specific numerical values (in millimetres) for a line speed of 200 km/h are contained within that EN standard and are not printed in the text of Regulation (EU) No 1299/2014 itself. Standard EN 13848-5:2008+A1:2010 (or the national track standards implementing it) should be consulted for the precise limit value.

question: How often must the track geometry recording car run over a high-speed line?
answer:
The corpus does not cover this question.

The EU acts in the corpus do not specify a mandatory frequency or schedule for running track geometry recording cars over high-speed (or other) lines. Instead, the Infrastructure TSI sets out the framework for track quality maintenance:

* Maintenance rules are developed within the procedures described in the infrastructure manager's safety management system [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5(1)].
* The infrastructure manager must draw up a maintenance plan for the subsystem to ensure TSI requirements are maintained during its lifetime [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5(3)].
* The maintenance file must contain at least a set of immediate action limit values and the measures to be taken when prescribed limits are not met [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5.1].

For specific track geometry inspection frequencies, check the infrastructure manager's internal maintenance plan, national safety rules approved by the relevant National Safety Authority, or applicable European standards (such as EN 13848-5).

(5) Instead of point (3), for the 1 520 mm track gauge system the Infrastructure Manager shall set out in the maintenance plan the base-length on which it will measure the track in order to check compliance with this requirement. (6) Instead of point (2), for the 1 668 mm track gauge system, the track twist limit is a function of the measurement base applied according to one of the following equations depending on the cant:

1. Each vehicle, before it is being used on the network, shall have an entity in charge of maintenance assigned to it and this entity shall be registered in the vehicle register in accordance with Article 47 of Directive (EU) 2016/797.

The corpus does not cover this question.

The EU acts in the corpus do not specify a mandatory frequency or schedule for running track geometry recording cars over high-speed (or other) lines. Instead, the Infrastructure TSI sets out the framework for track quality maintenance:

* Maintenance rules are developed within the procedures described in the infrastructure manager's safety management system [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5(1)].
* The infrastructure manager must draw up a maintenance plan for the subsystem to ensure TSI requirements are maintained during its lifetime [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5(3)].
* The maintenance file must contain at least a set of immediate action limit values and the measures to be taken when prescribed limits are not met [Reg_1299_2014, Annex, 4.5.1].

For specific track geometry inspection frequencies, check the infrastructure manager's internal maintenance plan, national safety rules approved by the relevant National Safety Authority, or applicable European standards (such as EN 13848-5).
